questions.q: What do the five letters in SARSA stand for?
options: State, Action, Reward, State, Action
Sample, Average, Reward, Sum, Average
State, Average, Return, Sample, Action
Sequential, Action, Reward, Sequential, Average
questions.explain: SARSA is named for the five quantities its update requires, in order: S_t, A_t, R_{t+1}, S_{t+1}, A_{t+1} — State, Action, Reward, State, Action.

questions.q: What is the single difference between the SARSA update and the Q-learning update?
options: SARSA does not use a discount factor
SARSA's target uses Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1}) — the actual next action taken — while Q-learning's target uses max_a Q(S_{t+1}, a)
SARSA requires a known model of the environment while Q-learning does not
SARSA can only be used on continuing tasks
questions.explain: Both updates share the same TD structure; the only difference is the target term — SARSA plugs in the Q-value of the action actually taken next, Q-learning plugs in the max over all possible next actions.

questions.q: Why does this one substitution make SARSA on-policy?
options: Because it removes the need for a reward signal
Because the target reflects the value of the policy actually being followed, including its exploration, rather than a separate greedy target policy
Because it requires episodic tasks only
Because it never uses epsilon-greedy exploration
questions.explain: By using the actually-chosen next action A_{t+1} in its target, SARSA is estimating the value of the exact policy generating the data — behavior policy and target policy coincide, which is the definition of on-policy.

questions.q: In the classic CliffWalking example, why does SARSA tend to learn a path further from the cliff edge than Q-learning?
options: SARSA cannot represent paths near the cliff at all

SARSA's update accounts for its own ongoing exploration (including accidentally stepping into the cliff), making it favor safer paths, while Q-learning's target always assumes the greedy action is taken
Q-learning always has a larger learning rate than SARSA
SARSA uses a different discount factor than Q-learning
questions.explain: SARSA's target incorporates the real possibility of exploratory missteps near the cliff, so it learns a policy value that reflects that risk, favoring a safer route; Q-learning's target assumes optimal (greedy) behavior and so favors the objectively shortest path.

questions.q: In a SARSA training loop, when must the next action A_{t+1} be chosen relative to the Q-value update?
options: After the update, using the new Q-values
Before the update is computed, since the update's target directly uses Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})
A_{t+1} is never actually needed — it is only hypothetical
At the very start of the episode only
questions.explain: SARSA's update formula requires Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1}), so the next action must be actually selected (e.g. via epsilon-greedy) before that value can be plugged into the update.
